working_title: Rainfall pulses increase frog active-community richness through species-selective reassembly
central_claims: Within matched route × seasonal-window comparisons, wetter runs contain more acoustically active species, and richness gain increases with rainfall contrast.
Rainfall-associated richness gain is not explained by simple nested addition; exact consecutive-year comparisons show increased compositional turnover with rainfall contrast.
Species wet-versus-dry recruitment responses are strongly heterogeneous and remain so after pair-level temperature, survey-date, rain-contrast magnitude, and year-gap adjustment.
Body size is a strong secondary predictor of species response in AmphiBIO: smaller-bodied species have more positive wet-recruitment responses, including after pair-level covariate adjustment.
pending_claims: Body-size effect persists under family-stratified permutation.
Body-size gradient can be independently validated in a second high-coverage trait source.
supporting_mechanism: Rain increases the number of acoustically active stops.
Rain increases run-level active species richness.
Within-active-stop and residual co-calling metrics show no detectable strengthening.
interpretation: Rainfall is associated with transient, species-selective reassembly of the acoustically active frog community rather than a uniform rise in activity by an unchanged assemblage.
prohibited: body size is the proven causal mechanism
temporary-water breeding strategy is directly tested unless an independent trait analysis is added
FrogID directly replicates the matched NAAMP community-reassembly result

evidence_status.body_size: secondary frozen trait-family discovery plus separately frozen adjusted-response robustness
